passages.t: God rescues the afflicted by their affliction
passages.happening:
‘And Elihu continued’ (verse 1). “Bear with me a little longer, and I will show you that there is more to be said on God’s behalf” (verse 2). He will ascribe justice to his Maker.

“Indeed, God is mighty, but He despises no one; He is mighty in strength of understanding” (verse 5). He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives justice to the afflicted, and he never takes his eyes off the righteous.

If people are bound in chains, caught in cords of affliction, God shows them what they have done and how proudly they have sinned. ‘He opens their ears to correction and commands that they turn from iniquity’ (verse 10). If they listen and serve him, they end their days in good years; if not, they perish without knowledge. The godless harbor resentment and do not cry out even when he binds them. ‘God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 36 and 37 are Elihu's fourth and last speech, the longest of the four. It gathers up his earlier themes, that God speaks through suffering and that God is perfectly just, and then turns toward God's greatness in creation.

Elihu's claim in verse 4 that one perfect in knowledge is with Job sounds arrogant, and some interpreters think the book means it to. Others note that the same phrase is used of God in 37:16 and suggest Elihu means only that his words are sound and wholehearted.

Verse 15 is the heart of his teaching. Affliction can be the very means by which God opens a person's ears and rescues them. Chains and captivity, in war or for debt, were common in that world, and fortunes could rise and fall quickly.
passages.later: A psalm says the same from the inside: “It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes” (Psalm 119:71).
passages.asks: Elihu said that God can open ears through trouble. Ask whether you have learned something in a hard season that you could not have learned in an easy one. And ask whether you hold that as your own story, without imposing it on someone else's.

passages.happening:
Elihu turns to Job. God drew him out of distress into a broad place, to a table full of rich food. ‘But now you are laden with the judgment due the wicked; judgment and justice have seized you’ (verse 17).

Let no one lure Job aside with riches or bribes. His wealth and effort cannot keep him from distress. “Do not long for the night, when people vanish from their homes. Be careful not to turn to iniquity, for this you have preferred to affliction” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew of verses 16 to 20 is notoriously difficult, and translations vary widely. Readers should hold any one rendering loosely.

What is clear is that Elihu applies his teaching pointedly to Job. Verse 17 says that Job is weighed down with the judgment due the wicked. That is the friends' charge again, put differently.
passages.hard:
Does God use suffering to teach? And can anyone say what he is teaching someone else?

Elihu says yes, at least sometimes. God binds people in cords of affliction to show them their pride and call them back. Many believers have found this true in their own lives, and Scripture supports it (Psalm 119:71). The danger is turning it into a universal explanation. Job's friends did that with punishment, and Elihu risks doing it with discipline, since he applies the teaching straight to Job in these verses.

The book as a whole resists that move. The reader knows from the prologue that Job's suffering was not caused by his pride and was not a lesson he needed. It was a test of whether faith can be real without reward. So the fairest answer is that suffering can become a means of God's teaching, and often does, but that no one is entitled to tell another sufferer what lesson God intends. Elihu's principle is true. His confidence about Job's case is the mistake.
passages.asks: Elihu was sure he knew what Job needed to learn. Ask whether you have ever said to someone in pain what God must be teaching them. And ask what you might have said instead.

passages.happening:
“Behold, God is exalted in His power. Who is a teacher like Him?” (verse 22). No one has set his way for him or told him he has done wrong. Job should praise God's work, which people have sung of.

‘Indeed, God is great’, ‘beyond our knowledge; the number of His years is unsearchable’ (verse 26). He draws up drops of water and distils rain from the mist, and the clouds pour it on mankind. Who can understand how the clouds spread out, or the thunder from his pavilion? He scatters his lightning and covers the depths of the sea. ‘For by these He judges the nations and provides food in abundance’ (verse 31). The thunder announces his presence, and even the cattle know the storm is rising.
passages.hearers:
Here Elihu turns from argument to hymn. Two cries of God's greatness, in verses 22 and 26, open two panels: God as the teacher without equal, and God in the rain and the storm.

Rain in the eastern Mediterranean falls mainly in autumn and winter, often in heavy storms, and the whole farming year depends on it. A failed rainy season meant hunger. When Elihu says that by the storm God judges the nations and gives food in abundance, he names the most important natural fact of life in that region: the same storm that terrifies also feeds.

By the end of the chapter Elihu is describing a gathering storm. Within two chapters, the LORD will answer Job out of the whirlwind.
passages.asks: Elihu ended in praise of a God beyond knowing. Ask when you last stood in front of something in creation and were simply amazed. And ask whether you can praise God for what you cannot understand.
